quests.instruction: Listen carefully and catch the exact sentence.
quests.hint: Catch whether one person or several people are involved.
quests.explanation: 'Has' marks a single subject while 'have' marks plural, but at speed both reduce to a quiet puff of air before the next word.
quests.textToSpeak: My manager has approved the request.
options: My managers have approved the request.
My manager has approved the request.

quests.instruction: They said it fast — what did you actually hear?
quests.hint: Listen for the exact number of times mentioned.
quests.explanation: 'Have' itself reduces to almost nothing here, so the detail that actually matters, how many times, sits in the words right after it.
quests.textToSpeak: We have visited that museum twice this year.
options: We have visited that museum once this year.
We have visited that museum twice this year.

quests.instruction: Natural speech blends words together. Catch the real message.
quests.hint: Notice who has the update, and what it actually says.
quests.explanation: 'Has' can blend almost silently into the subject before it, so keep listening past it for the real content, the update itself.
quests.textToSpeak: The team has released a new update today.
options: The team has released a new update yesterday.
The team has released a new update today.

quests.instruction: Listen for the small word that changes the meaning.
quests.hint: Catch whether this happened before or after the other event.
quests.explanation: 'Had' signals that one thing finished before another started, but it reduces to a light, fast sound that's easy to miss in a quick sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: By the time I arrived, they had already left.
options: By the time I arrived, they already left.
By the time I arrived, they had already left.

quests.instruction: Focus on the key detail hidden in the fast sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for what exactly had happened first.
quests.explanation: Once you catch the reduced 'had', the real content, what actually occurred earlier, is carried entirely by the verb that follows.
quests.textToSpeak: She had forgotten her umbrella at home.
options: She had forgotten her wallet at home.
She had forgotten her umbrella at home.

quests.instruction: Listen again — which version matches what was said?
quests.hint: Notice the order of events across the whole sentence.
quests.explanation: 'Had' places one action clearly before another, so the sequence itself is the thing being tested here, not just the individual words.
quests.textToSpeak: The film had already started when we got there.
options: The film hadn't started yet when we got there.
The film had already started when we got there.

quests.instruction: Listen carefully and catch the exact sentence.
quests.hint: Catch the exact action that's been completed.
quests.explanation: 'Have' links smoothly into the past participle that follows, almost like one word, so listen through the whole verb phrase, not just the start of it.
quests.textToSpeak: They have finally fixed the elevator.
options: They have finally fixed the elevator.
They have finally fixed the escalator.

quests.instruction: They said it fast — what did you actually hear?
quests.hint: Listen for whether this happened once or has never happened.
quests.explanation: 'Has never' reduces the auxiliary right into the negative word, so the whole phrase can sound like a quick blur unless you isolate 'never'.
quests.textToSpeak: He has never missed a deadline.
options: He missed a deadline.
He has never missed a deadline.

quests.instruction: Natural speech blends words together. Catch the real message.
quests.hint: Catch exactly what's been decided, not just that a decision exists.
quests.explanation: 'Have' collapses down fast before the verb, so hold your attention on the specific outcome named right after it.
quests.textToSpeak: We have decided to postpone the launch.
options: We have decided to postpone the launch.
We have decided to cancel the launch.

quests.instruction: Listen for the small word that changes the meaning.
quests.hint: Notice what had already gone wrong before the story starts.
quests.explanation: 'Had' plus a past participle points to something that happened even earlier than the rest of the story, and it reduces heavily at speed.
quests.textToSpeak: The printer had already jammed twice that morning.
options: The printer jammed twice that morning.
The printer had already jammed twice that morning.

quests.instruction: Focus on the key detail hidden in the fast sentence.
quests.hint: Catch the exact reason given for the delay.
quests.explanation: Once 'had' is caught, the specific cause that follows carries the real explanation — that's the detail worth focusing on here.
quests.textToSpeak: The flight was delayed because the crew had missed their connection.
options: The flight was delayed because the crew had missed their connection.
The flight was delayed because the crew had missed their briefing.

quests.instruction: Listen again — which version matches what was said?
quests.hint: Listen for whether the work was done in advance or not at all.
quests.explanation: 'Hadn't' squeezes a negative onto an already-reduced auxiliary, so this sentence tests two layers of listening at once.
quests.textToSpeak: They hadn't prepared the slides in advance.
options: They had prepared the slides in advance.
They hadn't prepared the slides in advance.

quests.instruction: Listen carefully and catch the exact sentence.
quests.hint: Catch what's actually happening right now, in progress.
quests.explanation: The progressive form links the reduced 'be' verb directly onto the '-ing' word, so the two run together almost as one sound at natural speed.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm currently reviewing your application.
options: I'm currently reviewing your application.
I currently reviewed your application.

quests.instruction: They said it fast — what did you actually hear?
quests.hint: Listen for exactly which task is in progress.
quests.explanation: Once the reduced 'is' or 'are' is caught, the real information, the activity itself, is entirely in the word that follows.
quests.textToSpeak: The team is still testing the new feature.
options: The team is still testing the old feature.
The team is still testing the new feature.

quests.instruction: Natural speech blends words together. Catch the real message.
quests.hint: Catch whether this is an ongoing action or a repeated habit.
quests.explanation: A progressive form describes something happening right now, while a simple form describes a routine — the difference hinges on a small, fast-reducing verb.
quests.textToSpeak: She's working late again tonight.
options: She works late again every night.
She's working late again tonight.

quests.instruction: Listen for the small word that changes the meaning.
quests.hint: Listen for the exact advice word, and which professional.
quests.explanation: 'Should' and 'could' both compress into a light, fast sound, but one gives firm advice while the other just offers a possibility.
quests.textToSpeak: You should see a specialist about that.
options: You should see a specialist about that.
You could see a specialist about that.

quests.instruction: Focus on the key detail hidden in the fast sentence.
quests.hint: Catch whether this is required or merely allowed.
quests.explanation: 'Must' expresses an obligation, while 'may' just permits something — both are short words that can be lost in a fast sentence if you're not listening closely.
quests.textToSpeak: Passengers must fasten their seatbelts now.
options: Passengers may fasten their seatbelts now.
Passengers must fasten their seatbelts now.

quests.instruction: Listen again — which version matches what was said?
quests.hint: Notice how sure the speaker sounds about this.
quests.explanation: 'Might' signals real uncertainty, while 'will' sounds confident — mixing them up completely changes how likely the speaker thinks this is.
quests.textToSpeak: It might rain later this afternoon.
options: It will rain later this afternoon.
It might rain later this afternoon.

quests.instruction: Listen carefully and catch the exact sentence.
quests.hint: Catch the reduced auxiliary at the very start of the question.
quests.explanation: 'Have you' often blurs into a quick 'ave-you' sound at natural speed, with the initial 'h' almost disappearing entirely.
quests.textToSpeak: Have you finished the report yet?
options: Have you finished the report yet?
Did you finish the report yet?

quests.instruction: They said it fast — what did you actually hear?
quests.hint: Listen for whether this question is about ability or permission.
quests.explanation: 'Can' and 'could' both shrink to a quick, light sound at the start of a question, but 'could' usually sounds a touch more formal or polite.
quests.textToSpeak: Could you send that file over?
options: Can you send that file over?
Could you send that file over?

quests.instruction: Natural speech blends words together. Catch the real message.
quests.hint: Catch whether they're asking about the past or checking right now.
quests.explanation: 'Did' and 'does' both reduce heavily, but one points to something already finished and the other to a current habit or fact.
quests.textToSpeak: Did she call the client back?
options: Did she call the client back?
Does she call the client back?

quests.instruction: Listen for the small word that changes the meaning.
quests.hint: Listen carefully for whether this is finished now or was finished earlier.
quests.explanation: 'Have' and 'had' differ by a single reduced vowel sound, but one places the action in the recent past and the other much further back.
quests.textToSpeak: We had already boarded when the delay was announced.
options: We have already boarded when the delay was announced.
We had already boarded when the delay was announced.

quests.instruction: Focus on the key detail hidden in the fast sentence.
quests.hint: Catch the tense first, then the specific detail that follows.
quests.explanation: This sentence hinges entirely on 'has' versus 'had' — both reduce fast, but only one keeps the story anchored to right now.
quests.textToSpeak: She has just landed at the airport.
options: She has just landed at the airport.
She had just landed at the airport.

quests.instruction: Listen again — which version matches what was said?
quests.hint: Notice whether the problem is still ongoing or already resolved earlier.
quests.explanation: 'Have fixed' means it's done as of now; 'had fixed' means it was already done before some other past moment — a subtle but real difference.
quests.textToSpeak: They have fixed the leak, so we're fine now.
options: They had fixed the leak, so we're fine now.
They have fixed the leak, so we're fine now.

quests.instruction: Listen carefully and catch the exact sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for how strongly this is being recommended.
quests.explanation: 'Should have' and 'could have' both reduce to a fast 'shoulda' or 'coulda' sound, but one is advice about a mistake and the other just a missed option.
quests.textToSpeak: You should have booked earlier.
options: You should have booked earlier.
You could have booked earlier.

quests.instruction: They said it fast — what did you actually hear?
quests.hint: Catch whether this was required, or simply possible.
quests.explanation: 'Must have' and 'might have' both compress heavily, but one states near-certainty about the past while the other only guesses.
quests.textToSpeak: He might have missed the announcement.
options: He must have missed the announcement.
He might have missed the announcement.

quests.instruction: Natural speech blends words together. Catch the real message.
quests.hint: Notice the exact level of confidence in the modal chosen.
quests.explanation: 'Would have' and 'wouldn't have' differ by that same small negative sound seen throughout this course — always worth a second listen.
quests.textToSpeak: I wouldn't have said that in the meeting.
options: I would have said that in the meeting.
I wouldn't have said that in the meeting.

quests.instruction: Listen for the small word that changes the meaning.
quests.hint: Track the full sequence: what had happened, what's happening now.
quests.explanation: This sentence blends 'had' and 'is' together, each reduced, each pointing to a different point in time — treat them as two separate checks.
quests.textToSpeak: The bags had already been checked, and boarding is starting now.
options: The bags had already been checked, and boarding is starting now.
The bags have already been checked, and boarding was starting now.

quests.instruction: Focus on the key detail hidden in the fast sentence.
quests.hint: Catch the modal, the auxiliary, and the actual detail together.
quests.explanation: By this level, a single sentence can combine a modal, a reduced auxiliary, and a specific detail — all three need to land for the full meaning to come through.
quests.textToSpeak: You could have mentioned that the meeting has been moved.
options: You could have mentioned that the meeting has been moved.
You should have mentioned that the meeting has been moved.

quests.instruction: Listen again — which version matches what was said?
quests.hint: Notice what was true before, and what's true right now.
quests.explanation: This sentence contrasts a past-perfect clause with a present progressive one, so the two different reduced auxiliaries need to be told apart clearly.
quests.textToSpeak: They hadn't noticed the error until it was already fixed.
options: They hadn't noticed the error until it was already fixed.
They haven't noticed the error until it was already fixed.
